newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spot natgas gains on cold Midwest weather.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spot natgas gains on cold Midwest weather.

text.p: U.S. spot natgas prices continued to rise in the Gulf and Midcontinent markets Monday as cold temperatures blanketed the Midwest and were forecast to move eastward midweek, sources said.
November gas on the Gulf Coast pipes was selling in the high-$3.60s to low-$3.70s as temperatures dove to as much as 30 degrees Fahrenheit below-normal in Texas.
December Gulf Coast prices were mostly steady in the low-$3.80s since nomination deadlines had expired, though there was discussion of notionally higher prices for swing gas.
Warmer temperatures are forecast to arrive to Texas later this week, as the cold weather heads toward the East.
The anticipated cold snap failed to lift New York city-gate prices for next month as traders reported closing deals around $4.70, down from Friday's $5.05-5.25 range.
For Tuesday delivery, city-gate gas sold mostly in the $4.30-4.35 area, sources said.
In the Midcontinent, a scramble for tight supplies pushed December prices more than 10 cents higher into the $3.80s, up an average of $1.30 from November 1 levels.
Next-day Midcontinent gas sold mostly in the $3.80s and $3.90s as the Texas and Midcontinent markets vied for the same supply.
Temperatures in the Midwest are expected to moderate by Wednesday or Thursday, forecasters said.

In west Texas, Permian prices for Tuesday delivery strengthened further to about $3.70, with Waha deals reported done early as high as $4.05. Same-day gas was also in high demand, causing prices to rise as high as $4.30.
Pacific Gas and Electric reported earlier Monday that its 1,087 megawatt Diablo Canyon 1 nuclear power unit would resume full service this Friday, a week after its automatic shutdown.
At the southern California border, the November and December markets were for the most part in convergence in the $3.75-3.90 range.
Sources attributed the softening in December prices at the border to more moderate weather in the West and weaker western Canadian prices.
